To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) children and adults are asymmetrically influenced by space and time in their judgments of distance and duration (2) children and adults show this asymmetry regardless of the linguistic frame used to elicit the judgments (3) children and adults do not show this asymmetry in judgments of distance and time when these are not represented in the same dimension.
children show the cross-dimensional asymmetry between space and time, and the asymmetry is robust across age and linguistic framing.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the relationship between space (a spatial dimension) and time (a temporal dimension) in the human mind.
the relationship between space-time representations and their implications for the development of analog magnitude representation.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the space-time asymmetry is present from early on in the life of the human mind.
space-time asymmetry in children is similar to that in adults.
the relationship between space-time representations is asymmetric and that the asymmetry is present in the child's mind as well as in the adult's mind.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
children and adults represent space and time in similar ways, and that these representations are asymmetric.
children, like adults, are more influenced by spatial than temporal information in their judgments of spatial and temporal distances.
the relationship between space-time representations is asymmetric in the developing mind, just as it is in the adult mind.
The main takeaway from our work is that

children are sensitive to the asymmetric relationship between space and temporal representations, which is in line with findings in adults and with the general idea that space is a more basic dimension than time.
